```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
source("../../_shared/template/viscount_rmd_helpers.R")
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

summary_data <- fromJSON("captaincy_general_guatemala_summary_cache.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
cfg_data <- read_json5_clean("captaincy_general_guatemala.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("captaincy_general_guatemala_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("captaincy_general_guatemala_source_ledger.json5")

clean_label <- function(x) {
  s <- as.character(x)
  s <- gsub("&", "and", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Intendencia de Leon \\(Nicaragua\\)", "Intendencia de León (Nicaragua)", s)
  s <- gsub("Audiencia de Panama, Veraguas", "Audiencia de Panamá, Veraguas", s)
  s <- gsub("Darien", "Darién", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Pérez Brign,", "Pérez Brignoli,", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("\\\\", "", s)
  trimws(s)
}

clean_level <- function(x) {
  s <- as.character(x)
  if (identical(s, "colonial_province")) return("Colonial Province")
  if (identical(s, "colonial_alcaldia_mayor")) return("Alcaldía Mayor or Corregimiento")
  if (identical(s, "colonial_governorship")) return("Colonial Governorship")
  if (identical(s, "colony")) return("British Settlement")
  gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
}

subregions <- summary_data$subregions
cfg_regions <- cfg_data$regions
cfg_by_id <- setNames(cfg_regions, vapply(cfg_regions, function(r) r$id, character(1)))
submask_counts <- ledger_data$saturation_audit$submask_coverage

tot_area <- as.numeric(summary_data$area_km2)
n_sites <- as.integer(summary_data$settlement_stats$total_settlements)
n_excluded <- as.integer(ledger_data$total_excluded)
tot_1600_krig <- as.numeric(summary_data$domain_trajectory[["1600"]])
tot_1700_krig <- as.numeric(summary_data$domain_trajectory[["1700"]])
tot_1780_krig <- as.numeric(summary_data$domain_trajectory[["1780"]])
tot_1800_krig <- as.numeric(summary_data$domain_trajectory[["1800"]])
tot_1820_krig <- as.numeric(summary_data$domain_trajectory[["1820"]])
```

# Abstract

Between Pedro de Alvarado's invasion of highland Guatemala in 1524 and the proclamation of Central American independence in 1821, the isthmian lands stretching from Chiapas to the Darién passed through one of the steepest demographic contractions and most uneven recoveries in the early modern Americas. Across eight territorial jurisdictions covering 682.861 km² (comprising the five core provinces of the Captaincy General of Guatemala, Ciudad Real de Chiapas, the unreduced Mosquitia Coast, the British Honduras logwood settlement and the trans-isthmian Audiencia of Panamá), archival demographic anchors place contact-era population at roughly 4,13M (4.125.000) in 1524 before epidemic waves, forced *encomienda* labour and the Nicaraguan-Honduran Indian slave trade drove aggregate numbers down by roughly 82% to a mid-seventeenth-century nadir near 742k in 1650 [@MacLeod1973; @Newson1986; @Newson1987; @Lovell1992]. Subsequent biological adaptation, highland *pueblo de indios* resilience, *mestizo* and *mulato* admixture (ladinoisation) and late-colonial export cycles in indigo, cattle, silver and mahogany lifted the archival provincial sum to 1,42M (1.420.200) by 1821, broadly matching the raster-integrated kriged substratum trajectory that rises from 519k in 1600 to 1,04M in 1700, peaks at 1,34M in 1800 and stands at 1,25M (1,83 inhabitants per km²) in 1820 [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Juarros1808; @JaenSuarez1978]. Yet growth remained profoundly asymmetric across altitude and coast: by the 1778 Bourbon census, the volcanic uplands and Pacific corridor from Chiapas through Guatemala and San Salvador to western Nicaragua held over four-fifths of the isthmus's Spanish-administered population, whereas the Caribbean lowlands of Petén (2.555), Portobelo (1.762), Darién (1.266) and British Honduras (3.824 in 1816) remained sparsely peopled maritime and forest frontiers [@Juarros1808; @JaenSuarez1978; @SIBBelize2024]. Integrating 21 provincial and sub-provincial Bourbon-era enumerations with a gazetteer of 190 geocoded settlements exhibiting a steep urban rank-size slope ($\alpha = 0,90$, $R^2 = 0,88$), this study reconciles archival headcounts, parish visitations and spatial kriging across three centuries of colonial isthmian history.

# Background

## Conquest, Epidemiological Shock and the Creation of the Audiencia

When Spanish expeditions converged on the Central American isthmus from both Mexico and Tierra Firme during the 1520s, they entered an ecologically fractured bridge linking Mesoamerican agrarian states to the circum-Caribbean chiefdoms of Lower Central America [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @MacLeod1973]. From the north, Pedro de Alvarado marched south through Soconusco in early 1524 to break the K'iche' and Kaqchikel polities of highland Guatemala before pushing into Pipil Cuscatlán (El Salvador), while Cristóbal de Olid, Hernán Cortés and rivals dispatched from Panamá contested Honduras and Nicaragua [@Lovell1992; @Newson1986]. From the south, Pedrarias Dávila had already founded Panamá on the Pacific coast in 1519 and dispatched Gil González Dávila and Francisco Hernández de Córdoba into the lake basins of Nicaragua, where León and Granada were established in 1524 [@Newson1987; @JaenSuarez1978].

The demographic catastrophe that followed was neither uniform nor purely military. Old World pathogens—above all smallpox (*viruela*), measles (*sarampión*), pneumonic plague, influenza and epidemic typhus (*matlazáhuatl* or *tabardillo*)—preceded Alvarado's columns into highland Guatemala around 1519–1521 and returned in punishing waves across the sixteenth century [@Lovell1992; @Medenou2025Mundo]. Mortality struck hardest in the hot, humid coastal lowlands of Soconusco, Pacific Guatemala, Fonseca, Nicaragua and Panamá, where malaria and yellow fever soon compounded respiratory epidemics [@MacLeod1973; @Newson1987]. In Nicaragua and southern Honduras, commercial slaving multiplied the biological toll: between 1524 and the enforcement of the New Laws in 1548–1550, Spanish merchants shipped tens of thousands of Chorotega, Nicarao and Lenca captives through Realejo and Nicoya to labour in the mines and estates of Peru and Panamá [@Newson1986; @Newson1987; @Newson2021Supervivencia].

Imperial administration struggled to impose order across these dispersed conquests. After an aborted beginning at Gracias a Dios in western Honduras in 1544—whose early urban grid still reflects its brief tenure as the first judicial seat of Central America [@Vinals2020Outstanding]—the Crown relocated the Audiencia de los Confines to Santiago de Guatemala in 1549. Renamed the Audiencia and Captaincy General of Guatemala, its jurisdiction stretched from the Alcaldía Mayor of Ciudad Real de Chiapas (which remained tied to Guatemala until 1824) southward to Costa Rica, while Panamá, Veraguas and Darién formed a separate Audiencia of Panamá attached first to the Viceroyalty of Peru and after 1739 to New Granada [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @JaenSuarez1978]. In administrative reality, however, Spanish authority hugged the Pacific volcanic chain and cool intermontane basins; nearly the entire Caribbean littoral from Belize to eastern Nicaragua and Darién remained an unreduced zone of indigenous autonomy, runaway enslaved Africans (*cimarrones*) and English privateers [@Newson1986; @Wainwright2020Colonial].

## Cacao Booms, Indigo Cycles and Highland Congregaciones

Over the two centuries following conquest, Central America's population geography was reshaped by two opposing forces: forced resettlement of surviving indigenous communities in the highlands and sequential export booms along the Pacific piedmont [@MacLeod1973; @Lovell1992]. Beginning in the 1540s and accelerating through the 1570s, Dominican, Franciscan and Mercedarian friars gathered scattered Maya hamlets (*parcialidades*) into nucleated *pueblos de indios* laid out around a church plaza. In the Cuchumatán highlands of Huehuetenango, the K'iche' and Kaqchikel basins of Totonicapán, Sololá and Chimaltenango, the Q'eqchi' valleys of Verapaz and the Tzotzil-Tzeltal uplands of Chiapas, *congregación* initially exposed concentrated villagers to fresh typhus and measles outbreaks [@Lovell1992; @Medenou2025Mundo]. Over the longer run, however, corporate village charters, communal *ejidos* and indigenous *cabildos* led by hereditary *principales* provided an institutional shield against total land dispossession and sustained Maya demographic persistence—and linguistic continuity—into the nineteenth century [@Cruz1999Lite; @Sanchez2015Tedras; @Quijas2012Interpretaciones].

Down on the warm Pacific littoral, commercial agriculture followed a harsher boom-and-bust rhythm. From the 1540s through the 1580s, Soconusco, Suchitepéquez and Izalco (Sonsonate) supplied Mexico City with prized cacao beans grown on indigenous orchards and tapped through heavy tribute assessments [@MacLeod1973]. As coastal labourers died out faster than highland migrants could replace them, the cacao boom collapsed after 1600, giving way to a century-long depression across much of the Captaincy General. Spanish landowners turned instead to cattle ranching in Choluteca, Olancho, Nicaragua and Guanacaste, small-scale silver extraction around Tegucigalpa and Comayagua, and above all the cultivation of *añil* (indigo) across the volcanic foothills of San Salvador, San Vicente and San Miguel [@MacLeod1973; @Wortman1982]. Because indigo processing required intense seasonal labour during the August-to-October harvest (*obrajes*), royal prohibitions against forced indigenous dye-work encouraged planters to recruit *ladino*, *mestizo* and *mulato* wage labourers and sharecroppers, transforming El Salvador into the most densely settled mixed-race province of colonial Central America [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Osegueda2024Migrar].

## Capital Earthquakes, Ladinoisation and Bourbon Reforms

At the centre of this colonial hierarchy stood Santiago de Guatemala (modern Antigua Guatemala), rebuilt in the Panchoy Valley after the 1541 lahar destroyed the earlier capital at Ciudad Vieja. Across two centuries, Santiago grew into the undisputed metropolis of the isthmus, climbing from 9,4k inhabitants in 1574 to 24,5k in 1646, 34,2k in 1700 and a pre-catastrophe peak of 37,5k in 1768 [@Lutz1994; @Juarros1808]. As Christopher Lutz demonstrated from parish marriage and baptismal registers, Santiago functioned as a demographic crucible in which urban Spaniards, highland Maya *naborías*, enslaved and free Africans and *castas* intermarried across parish boundaries, driving steady *ladinoisation* long before the late-colonial census era [@Lutz1994; @Contributors2014Pathways]. That urban primacy suffered a dramatic rupture on 29 July 1773, when the Santa Marta earthquake levelled Santiago's churches, convents and royal palaces. Despite fierce opposition from entrenched landowners and clergy, Captain General Martín de Mayorga forced the relocation of the capital to the Ermita Valley, formally founding Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción (Ciudad de Guatemala) in January 1776 [@Lutz1994; @Wortman1982]. By 1778 the new capital already held 23.434 residents, expanding to 31,5k by 1820, while battered Antigua retained roughly 11,2k inhabitants by 1808.

The relocation coincided with the peak of Bourbon administrative and statistical reform. Between 1768 and 1770, Archbishop Pedro Cortés y Larraz conducted an exhaustive parish-by-parish *visita* of the Archdiocese of Guatemala (encompassing Guatemala and El Salvador), documenting scattered *valles* of unregulated *ladino* squatters alongside traditional Maya parishes [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Osegueda2024Migrar]. In 1778 the Crown ordered the first empire-wide population census, whose Central American returns were later preserved and refined by Domingo Juarros in his 1808 *Compendio* [@Juarros1808], and in 1785–1787 Madrid reorganised the provinces outside core Guatemala into four *intendencias*: Ciudad Real de Chiapas, San Salvador, Comayagua (Honduras) and León (Nicaragua, with Costa Rica remaining a subordinate governorship) [@Wortman1982]. Yet Bourbon fiscal centralisation and the wartime disruption of Atlantic indigo shipping after 1796 strained provincial loyalties, setting the economic stage for the peaceful separation from Spain in September 1821 and the subsequent break-up of the Kingdom of Guatemala [@Wortman1982; @Osegueda2024Migrar].

## Unreduced Atlantic Frontiers, British Honduras and the Isthmus of Panamá

Outside the Spanish Pacific spine, three distinctive colonial frontiers followed divergent demographic trajectories. Along the humid Caribbean coast from Trujillo and Black River (Palacios) past Cabo Gracias a Dios to Bluefields and Pearl Lagoon, indigenous Sumu, Pech, Rama and coastal Miskitu communities remained outside Spanish tribute rolls throughout the colonial era [@Newson1986; @Newson1987]. Beginning in the mid-seventeenth century, intermarriage between coastal Miskitu bands and shipwrecked or escaped enslaved Africans produced the *Zambo-Miskitu* polity, whose leaders forged an enduring commercial and military alliance with British Jamaica. Armed with English muskets, Miskitu raiders extracted tribute from interior riverine groups, raided Spanish cacao estates in Matina (Costa Rica) and sustained an autonomous Mosquito Kingdom whose diplomatic authority outlasted Spanish rule into the nineteenth century [@Newson2021Supervivencia; @Clavel2026King].

Immediately northwest along the Bay of Honduras, English buccaneers and woodcutters established seasonal logwood (*Haematoxylum campechianum*) camps at the mouth of the Belize River during the mid-seventeenth century, shifting to mahogany extraction after the 1763 Treaty of Paris and the 1786 Convention of London [@Wainwright2020Colonial; @Gali2026Historical]. Although Spanish authorities repeatedly expelled the Baymen—most destructively in 1779 before the decisive British naval defence at St. George's Caye in 1798—the settlement consolidated around Belize Town, Corozal and Orange Walk using a predominantly enslaved African timber workforce documented in British muster rolls from 1790 onward (2.656 in Belize Town in 1790, rising to 3.824 across the colony in 1816 and 4.163 in Belize Town by 1820) [@SIBBelize2024]. Between 1797 and 1802, a new maritime people reshaped the southern coast of Honduras and Belize: following Britain's deportation of roughly 2.000 Black Caribs (Garifuna) from St. Vincent to Roatán in 1797, Garifuna families settled Trujillo, coastal Honduras and Stann Creek (Dangriga) in southern Belize, laying the demographic foundation of the modern Gulf of Honduras littoral [@Wainwright2020Colonial; @SIBBelize2024].

At the southeastern neck of the isthmus, the Audiencia of Panamá operated under an altogether different imperial logic. Rather than highland tribute or export crops, Panamá lived off silver transit between Peru and Seville via the *Camino Real* and the Chagres River to Portobelo [@JaenSuarez1978]. Because transit commerce depended on urban merchants, muleteers, free *pardos* and enslaved Africans—supported by rice and cattle provisioning from Natá, Los Santos, Penonomé and Veraguas [@Aram2021Rice]—Panamá's population fluctuated sharply with imperial trade cycles. Henry Morgan's sack of Panamá Viejo in 1671 forced the city's relocation to the fortified Casco Antiguo peninsula in 1673, while Admiral Edward Vernon's destruction of Portobelo in 1739 and the Crown's abolition of the Tierra Firme galleon fleet ended the *ferias*, plunging the trans-isthmian corridor into protracted stagnation until late-eighteenth-century agricultural growth in the Azuero Peninsula and Chiriquí lifted the Panamanian provinces toward 92k inhabitants by 1821 [@JaenSuarez1978].

# Methodology

## Jurisdictional Partition of the Eight Colonial Sub-Regions

To reconcile Spanish colonial administrative enumerations with trans-border ecological continuity across 1524 to 1821, our spatial mask partitions Central America, Chiapas, Belize and Panamá into eight contiguous jurisdictions totalling 682.861,1 km² on the equal-area projection. Rather than imposing twentieth-century national boundaries backward onto the colonial era, the polygons align directly with late-eighteenth-century *intendencias*, *gobernaciones* and unreduced frontier zones preserved in the Historical GIS of the Indies and historical atlases [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Wortman1982].

The northern tier comprises two highland-and-lowland Maya complexes alongside the Caribbean timber enclave: the Intendencia de Ciudad Real de Chiapas (74.626,2 km², administratively subordinate to Guatemala until 1824), the Provincia de Guatemala Core and Verapaz (175.682 km², uniting the central highlands, Pacific piedmont, Chiquimula, Verapaz and the frontier *partido* of Petén) and the British Honduras Logwood Settlement (13.975,3 km², covering the Belize, New and Hondo river catchments). The central isthmus separates the compact Pacific indigo belt of the Intendencia de San Salvador and Sonsonate (20.857 km²) and the silver-and-cattle interior of the Intendencia de Comayagua in Honduras (77.147,6 km²) from the vast, unreduced Caribbean watershed of the Mosquitia Coast (122.699,3 km², spanning historical Taguzgalpa and Tologalpa from eastern Honduras through eastern Nicaragua). The southern tier pairs the Pacific volcanic-and-central-valley corridor of the Intendencia de León (Nicaragua) and Costa Rica (110.817,3 km²) with the trans-isthmian Audiencia de Panamá, Veraguas and Darién (87.056,4 km²).

## Dual Calibration: Archival Benchmarks and Raster-Kriged Substrata

Colonial Central American demography presents a classic archival asymmetry: tribute counts (*tasaciones*) survive sporadically for the sixteenth century, parish visitations and ecclesiastical counts thicken after 1680, and near-universal Bourbon provincial censuses arrive only in 1778–1796 [@Lovell1992; @Juarros1808; @JaenSuarez1978]. To track both the sixteenth-century demographic collapse and the continuous decadal trajectory from 1600 to 1820 without obscuring uncertainty, this study integrates two complementary series.

First, an archival historical-demography anchor table specifies point-in-time population totals $P^{\text{arch}}_r(t)$ across all eight jurisdictions at 1524 (conquest contact), 1650 (colonial demographic trough), 1778 or 1790 (Bourbon and British muster censuses), 1800 and 1821 (independence eve). These anchors synthesise regional historical-demographic monographs for Guatemala [@Lovell1992; @Lutz1994], Honduras [@Newson1986], Nicaragua [@Newson1987; @Newson2021Supervivencia], Costa Rica [@PerezBrignoli2010; @Leon2003Cata], Panamá [@JaenSuarez1978], Chiapas [@Cruz1999Lite] and British Honduras [@SIBBelize2024], cross-checked against Juarros's 1778 provincial returns [@Juarros1808] and Hall and Pérez Brignoli's isthmian synthesis [@HallPerezBrignoli2003].

Second, for continuous decadal mapping from 1600 to 1820, gridded regional population surfaces are integrated across each jurisdictional mask polygon $r$ of pixel-measured area $A_r$ using Matérn spatial kriging conditioned on historical land-use and settlement priors:

$$P^{\text{krig}}_r(t) = \sum_{j \in \Omega_r} \hat{\rho}_j(t) \cdot a_j, \qquad d^{\text{krig}}_r(t) = \frac{P^{\text{krig}}_r(t)}{A_r}$$

where $\Omega_r$ denotes the set of equal-area raster cells inside jurisdiction $r$, $a_j$ is cell area in km² and $\hat{\rho}_j(t)$ is the estimated local population density at decadal step $t \in \{1600, 1700, 1710, \dots, 1820\}$. Inter-benchmark compound annual growth rates follow standard geometric compounding:

$$g_r(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

Explicitly tabulating both $P^{\text{arch}}_r(t)$ and $P^{\text{krig}}_r(t)$ allows quantitative evaluation of where smooth gridded priors accurately capture aggregate isthmian growth and where coarse raster smoothing leaks population from compact highland valleys into adjacent low-density Caribbean lowlands.

## Sub-Administrative Census Ingestion and Settlement Gazetteer Assembly

To anchor sub-provincial demography beyond aggregate regional polygons, we compiled 21 primary Bourbon-era and British colonial administrative counts spanning 1778 to 1816. These records preserve the five main Audiencia provincial totals of 1778 (Guatemala, San Salvador and Sonsonate, León, Comayagua and Costa Rica), eleven constituent *alcaldías mayores*, *corregimientos* and *partidos* of core Guatemala (from Chiquimula and Totonicapán down to Petén), four colonial governorships of Panamá (Panamá, Veraguas, Portobelo and Darién) and the 1816 colonial muster of British Honduras [@Juarros1808; @HallPerezBrignoli2003; @JaenSuarez1978; @SIBBelize2024].

At the town and parish scale, our settlement gazetteer catalogues `r viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L)` geocoded places spanning 1574 to 1820 across all eight modern national territories (95 in Chiapas/Mexico, 43 in Panamá, 13 in Nicaragua, 11 in Guatemala, 10 in Honduras, 7 in El Salvador, 6 in Costa Rica and 5 in Belize). Source-ledger auditing tracked four sequential ingestion waves: Wave 1 assembled 173 primary official and archival town records from the Historical GIS of the Indies (drawing directly on the 1774–1796 Chiapas parish reports, 1778 Panamanian and Veraguas censuses, Cortés y Larraz's 1770 *visita* and Juarros's 1808 *Compendio*); Wave 2 added 12 peer-reviewed demographic monograph series covering Nicaragua, Honduras, Panamá and British Honduras; Wave 3 backfilled 3 longitudinal colonial series; and Wave 4 executed a sub-regional gap-verification sweep adding 2 frontier settlements (marginal gain 1,06%, confirming source saturation with a 0% crowd-sourced share). Spatial deduplication across 196 candidate records merged `r viscount_fmt_number(n_excluded, 0L)` duplicate alias records within 25 km buffers (Antigua Guatemala, Panamá, Tuxtla, Tapachula, Ciudad Real de Chiapas and David).

To test urban primacy and spatial integration across the isthmus, we fit an ordinary least-squares Zipf rank-size regression on log-transformed settlement populations across the top 95 ranked towns of the 190-settlement register (using the 1774 cross-section):

$$\log_{10} P_{(k)} = c - \alpha \log_{10} k$$

where $P_{(k)}$ is the population of the $k$-th largest town and $\alpha$ measures hierarchy steepness.

# Testing and Validation

## Reconciliation of Archival Provincial Anchors Against Raster-Kriged Surfaces

Table \ref{tab:subregion-benchmarks} juxtaposes the archival historical-demography trajectory (1524, 1650, 1778 or 1790 and 1821) against the raster-integrated kriged 1820 population and catalogued settlement counts across all eight jurisdictions. On the aggregate isthmian scale, the two independent reconstructions converge tightly at the end of the colonial era: the archival provincial sum stands at 1,42M (1.420.200) in 1821, whereas the raster-kriged domain total reaches 1,34M in 1800 and 1,25M (1.248.656) in 1820—an aggregate difference of 12,1% well within colonial enumeration error bounds [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Wortman1982].

```{r tab-subregion-benchmarks, results='asis'}
bench_rows <- lapply(subregions, function(r) {
  rid <- r$id
  cfg_r <- cfg_by_id[[rid]]
  p_arch <- cfg_r$population
  a_krig <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p1524 <- as.numeric(p_arch[["1524"]])
  p1650 <- as.numeric(p_arch[["1650"]])
  p1778 <- if (!is.null(p_arch[["1778"]])) as.numeric(p_arch[["1778"]]) else as.numeric(p_arch[["1790"]])
  p1821 <- as.numeric(p_arch[["1821"]])
  p1820_k <- as.numeric(r$end_pop)
  sc <- submask_counts[[rid]]
  sc_val <- if (is.null(sc)) 0L else as.integer(sc)
  data.frame(
    Subregion = clean_label(r$name),
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(a_krig), 0L),
    P1524 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1524),
    P1650 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1650),
    P1778 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1778),
    P1821 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1821),
    P1820K = viscount_fmt_pop(p1820_k),
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(sc_val, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bench <- do.call(rbind, bench_rows)

sum_1524 <- sum(vapply(subregions, function(r) as.numeric(cfg_by_id[[r$id]]$population[["1524"]]), numeric(1)))
sum_1650 <- sum(vapply(subregions, function(r) as.numeric(cfg_by_id[[r$id]]$population[["1650"]]), numeric(1)))
sum_1778 <- sum(vapply(subregions, function(r) {
  p <- cfg_by_id[[r$id]]$population
  if (!is.null(p[["1778"]])) as.numeric(p[["1778"]]) else as.numeric(p[["1790"]])
}, numeric(1)))
sum_1821 <- sum(vapply(subregions, function(r) as.numeric(cfg_by_id[[r$id]]$population[["1821"]]), numeric(1)))

df_tot <- data.frame(
  Subregion = "Isthmian Domain Total (8 Jurisdictions)",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(tot_area), 0L),
  P1524 = viscount_fmt_pop(sum_1524),
  P1650 = viscount_fmt_pop(sum_1650),
  P1778 = viscount_fmt_pop(sum_1778),
  P1821 = viscount_fmt_pop(sum_1821),
  P1820K = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1820_krig),
  Sites = viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_bench <- rbind(df_bench, df_tot)
rownames(df_bench) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_bench,
  "Archival demographic anchors (1524, 1650, 1778 or 1790 and 1821), raster-kriged 1820 totals and catalogued settlement counts across eight colonial isthmian jurisdictions.",
  c("Colonial Jurisdiction", "Area (km²)", "1524 Arch.", "1650 Nadir", "1778/90 Arch.", "1821 Arch.", "1820 Raster", "Sites"),
  list(label = "tab:subregion-benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Closer sub-regional testing, however, uncovers an instructive spatial-allocation divergence between the archival census anchors and the raster-kriged surface. In four jurisdictions—Ciudad Real de Chiapas (118k archival in 1821 vs. 108,2k raster in 1820), Comayagua in Honduras (135k vs. 108,5k), León and Costa Rica (235k vs. 197,8k) and Panamá, Veraguas and Darién (92k vs. 120,8k)—the two series sit within a modest 8% to 31% band. By contrast, along the sharp topographic divide separating the Pacific volcanic highlands from the Caribbean rainforest, coarse global raster interpolation visibly bleeds population eastward. Specifically, the raster surface assigns 229,3k to the Mosquitia Coast and 43,4k to British Honduras in 1820, whereas colonial musters, missionary accounts and ethnohistorical reconstructions place Mosquitia near 52k and British Honduras at 5,2k (3.824 enumerated in 1816) [@SIBBelize2024; @Newson1986; @Newson1987]. Symmetrically, the raster surface under-allocates the hyper-compact volcanic corridor of San Salvador and Sonsonate (79k raster in 1820 vs. 248k archival in 1821) and core Guatemala (361,7k raster vs. 535k archival).

This cross-check confirms an essential rule for colonial Central American historical geography: while the raster-kriged substratum faithfully tracks long-run macro-isthmian recovery between 1600 and 1820, sub-provincial density gradients across steep cordilleran divides must be anchored directly to Bourbon census rolls, ecclesiastical *visitas* and local archival registers [@Juarros1808; @HallPerezBrignoli2003; @JaenSuarez1978].

## Cross-Checks Against Colonial Demographic Historiography

Our archival 1524–1821 envelope aligns closely with regional demographic scholarship while avoiding both the extreme low counts of mid-twentieth-century skeptics and speculative ultra-high projections. For Honduras, Linda Newson estimated an aboriginal contact population of roughly 800k (split between western chiefdoms and eastern Taguzgalpa) collapsing by more than 90% into the seventeenth century before recovering toward 130k–140k by independence; our partitioned anchors—420k for Intendencia de Comayagua plus a substantial fraction of the 160k assigned to the Mosquitia Coast in 1524, rebounding to 135k in Comayagua by 1821—track that trajectory closely [@Newson1986]. For Nicaragua, Newson's detailed reassessment placed contact population above 800k across the densely farmed Pacific lakes and Nicoya, falling below 100k in the seventeenth century due to combined slave exports and epidemics before climbing back toward 180k–200k by 1821; combining Nicaragua with Costa Rica yields our 890k contact benchmark, 95k nadir in 1650, 131,2k in 1778 and 235k in 1821 [@Newson1987; @Newson2021Supervivencia; @PerezBrignoli2010].

In highland Guatemala, W. George Lovell documented an indigenous collapse of roughly 85% to 90% in the Cuchumatán Sierra between 1520 and 1670 followed by sustained eighteenth-century recovery that restored highland densities despite recurring typhus and smallpox shocks in 1733, 1780 and 1802 [@Lovell1992; @Medenou2025Mundo]. Our core Guatemala trajectory—1,25M in 1524 to 260k in 1650 (-79,2%), recovering to 366k–398,6k in 1778 and 535k by 1821 (+0,42% per annum from 1650 to 1821)—fits securely within Lovell and Lutz's consensus bounds [@Lovell1992; @Lutz1994]. In Panamá, Omar Jaén Suárez reconstructed an early-sixteenth-century population of roughly 400k–500k devastated by Pedrarias Dávila's *entradas* and tropical disease, sinking to barely 59k enumerated colonial residents across the four governorships in 1778 (68k including unreduced Darién and coastal indigenous groups) and rising to roughly 92k by 1821 [@JaenSuarez1978].

# Results

## Isthmian Demographic Trajectory: Collapse, Trough and Bourbon Recovery

Taken across the full three-century span from 1524 to 1821, Central American demographic history falls into three starkly contrasting epochs. First came the sixteenth-century catastrophe (1524 to 1650), during which the archival isthmian total plunged from 4,13M to 742k—a net loss of 3,38M inhabitants (-82,0%, or -1,35% per annum over 126 years) [@MacLeod1973; @Lovell1992; @Medenou2025Mundo]. Lowland provinces suffered the deepest contraction: León and Costa Rica dropped 89,3% (from 890k to 95k), Panamá fell 84,8% (from 540k to 82k), Comayagua fell 82,9% (from 420k to 72k) and San Salvador fell 81,5% (from 460k to 85k), whereas highland Guatemala retained a slightly larger surviving base (-79,2%, from 1,25M to 260k) and the remote Mosquitia Coast experienced a gentler initial drop (-70,0%, from 160k to 48k) owing to sparse Spanish penetration [@Newson1986; @Newson1987].

Second came a century of tentative biological stabilisation and uneven demographic rebound from 1650 to 1760. Figure \ref{fig:guatemala-trajectory} illustrates the continuous raster-integrated trajectory from 1600 to 1820 alongside sub-regional 1820 raster densities. Across the seventeenth century, aggregate raster totals climbed from 519k in 1600 to 1,04M in 1700, dipped sharply to 929,7k in 1710 during early-eighteenth-century epidemic and cacao-depression shocks, and then climbed steadily through 1,03M (1730) and 1,16M (1750) before plateauing around 1,13M to 1,16M between 1760 and 1780 [@MacLeod1973; @Wortman1982].

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/captaincy_general_guatemala_population_trajectory.png",
  "Raster-integrated demographic trajectory for colonial Central America and its four largest kriged sub-regions from 1600 to 1820 (Panel A) and sub-regional raster densities in 1820 (Panel B).",
  "fig:guatemala-trajectory"
)
```

Third came the late-colonial Bourbon acceleration (1778 to 1821). Archival provincial sums rose from 918,7k in 1778–1790 to 1,42M in 1821—a gain of +54,6% in barely four decades (+1,02% per annum, more than triple the 1650–1778 recovery rate of +0,17% per annum). San Salvador and Sonsonate led that surge at +1,23% per annum (146,7k in 1778 to 248k in 1821), followed closely by León and Costa Rica at +1,36% per annum (131,2k to 235k), Ciudad Real de Chiapas at +1,25% per annum (69,3k to 118k), Comayagua at +1,01% per annum (87,7k to 135k) and core Guatemala at +0,89% per annum (366k to 535k) [@Wortman1982; @HallPerezBrignoli2003; @PerezBrignoli2010]. Across the entire domain, the raster surface confirms a late-colonial peak of 1,34M in 1800 before late-colonial locust plagues, indigo trade collapse during the Napoleonic Wars and smallpox outbreaks trimmed growth between 1800 and 1820 [@Wortman1982; @Osegueda2024Migrar].

## The 1778 to 1816 Bourbon and Colonial Census Architecture

The documentary bedrock of late-colonial Central American demography is the 1778 imperial census—supplemented by Panamanian governorship counts of the same year and the 1816 British Honduras muster. Table \ref{tab:hgis-subadmin} prints all 21 administrative enumerations compiled in the chapter's sub-administrative census register, exposing the fine-grained spatial distribution of the isthmian population inside the Kingdom of Guatemala and its bordering colonies [@Juarros1808; @HallPerezBrignoli2003; @JaenSuarez1978; @SIBBelize2024].

```{r tab-hgis-subadmin, results='asis'}
hgis_list <- summary_data$hgis_subadmin_table
hgis_rows <- lapply(hgis_list, function(h) {
  data.frame(
    Unit = clean_label(h$unit_name),
    Territory = as.character(h$country),
    Level = clean_level(h$level),
    Year = as.character(as.integer(h$year)),
    Pop = viscount_fmt_number(as.integer(h$population), 0L),
    Source = clean_label(h$source),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_hgis <- do.call(rbind, hgis_rows)
rownames(df_hgis) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_hgis,
  "Bourbon provincial, sub-provincial and British colonial census enumerations across Central America, Panama and Belize, 1778 to 1816 (21 administrative units).",
  c("Administrative Unit", "Modern Territory", "Jurisdiction Level", "Year", "Population", "Primary Source"),
  list(label = "tab:hgis-subadmin", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 25L)
)
```

Disaggregating the 1778 Kingdom of Guatemala returns reveals a striking geographical concentration. Across the five core Central American provinces enumerated in 1778 (excluding Chiapas), the Province of Guatemala alone held 398.575 inhabitants—53,4% of the 746.086-person five-province total—followed almost neck-and-neck by San Salvador and Sonsonate (117.436; rising to 146.684 once full Sonsonate and scattered *valles* are reconciled in the archival anchor) and the Intendancy of León covering Nicaragua and Nicoya (117.396), ahead of Comayagua in Honduras (88.143) and the thinly settled Governorship of Costa Rica (24.536) [@Juarros1808; @HallPerezBrignoli2003].

Inside Guatemala proper, eleven constituent *alcaldías mayores* and *corregimientos* account for 369.164 inhabitants in Table \ref{tab:hgis-subadmin}, pinpointing the demographic heartland of colonial Mesoamerica south of Oaxaca. Five densely peopled highland and eastern districts each surpassed 40k residents: the eastern *ladino* and Ch'orti' Corregimiento de Chiquimula (52.423), the K'iche' highland Alcaldía Mayor de Totonicapán (51.272), the metropolitan peri-urban valleys of Sacatepéquez (50.786), the Q'eqchi' and Poqomchi' Alcaldía Mayor de la Verapaz (49.583) and the Kaqchikel plateau of Chimaltenango (40.082). A second tier between 17k and 29k encompassed Quezaltenango (28.563), Sololá around Lake Atitlán (27.953), coastal Escuintla (24.978), newly founded Ciudad de Guatemala (23.434) and cacao-producing Suchitepéquez (17.535). By contrast, the vast northern rainforest of Partido del Petén—finally conquered from the Itza Maya at Nojpetén (Flores) only in 1697—held barely 2.555 Spanish-administered inhabitants in 1778, less than 0,7% of Guatemala's population across nearly a third of its territory [@Juarros1808; @Lovell1992].

## Highland Maya Core: Guatemala and Ciudad Real de Chiapas

Throughout the colonial centuries, the highland corridor running from San Cristóbal (Ciudad Real de Chiapas) through Huehuetenango, Totonicapán, Quetzaltenango, Sololá and Chimaltenango to Cobán remained the demographic anchor of Central America. Unlike the Caribbean coast or the Pacific sugar and cacao plains, elevations between 1.500 m and 2.500 m excluded endemic *falciparum* malaria and yellow fever, allowing highland Maya villages to absorb periodic typhus and smallpox losses and rebound naturally [@Lovell1992; @Medenou2025Mundo]. In the Western Highlands and Verapaz, *pueblos de indios* retained corporate land titles, cofradía treasuries and bilingual ecclesiastical administration; chairs of Kaqchikel and K'iche' established at the University of San Carlos in Guatemala during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries reflected the enduring demographic weight of indigenous-speaking parishes [@Sanchez2015Tedras; @Quijas2012Interpretaciones].

A parallel structure operated in the Intendencia de Ciudad Real de Chiapas, which remained judicially and commercially bound to Guatemala throughout the colonial era before opting for union with Mexico in 1824. Although Chiapas's contact population of roughly 390k collapsed to 92k by 1650 and sank further to 69.253 in the 1778 census following the 1712 Tzeltal Rebellion and mid-century famine, late-colonial recovery carried the intendancy to 98k by 1800 and 118k by 1821 [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Cruz1999Lite]. Remarkably, Chiapas's urban network remained overwhelmingly indigenous and rural in character: whereas the Spanish capital of Ciudad Real de Chiapas held 5,8k inhabitants in 1814 and lowland Tuxtla held 5,4k, the surrounding Tzotzil and Tzeltal *pueblos* governed by indigenous *principales*—led by Chamula (11.695 in 1796), Comitán (8.174), San Bartolomé (7.410) and Santo Domingo Oxchuc (7.314)—outnumbered the provincial Spanish seat [@Cruz1999Lite].

## Indigo Heartlands, Silver Uplands and Pastoral Frontiers

South and east of Guatemala, colonial demography shifted rapidly from highland Maya majorities toward *mestizo*, *mulato* and *ladino* populations shaped by export commodities and mobility [@Osegueda2024Migrar]. Compact San Salvador and Sonsonate (only 20.857 km² on the regional mask) emerged by 1821 as the most densely settled province of Central America: its archival density reached 13,46 inhabitants per km² on its 18.430 km² administrative area (and even on the smoothed raster surface in Figure \ref{fig:guatemala-trajectory} Panel B, San Salvador led all eight sub-regions at 3,79 inhabitants per km²). Centred on San Salvador (16,5k in 1820), Santa Ana (10,8k), San Miguel (8,9k), San Vicente (7,1k) and Sonsonate (6,9k), the province's dense belt of indigo estates, maize smallholdings and commercial fairs drew constant migrant streams from neighbouring Guatemala and Honduras [@MacLeod1973; @Wortman1982; @Osegueda2024Migrar].

To the north, the Intendencia de Comayagua (Honduras) remained far more dispersed across rugged pine-oak mountains and intermontane basins. Following the sixteenth-century gold-washing frenzy and Indian slave exports, Spanish Honduras stalled near 72k in 1650 before growing modestly to 87.730 in 1778 and 135k by 1821 [@Newson1986]. Two rival poles anchored the province: the conservative ecclesiastical and administrative capital of Comayagua (8,9k in 1820) and the livelier silver-mining centre of Tegucigalpa (8,65k), complemented by western tobacco and cattle districts around Santa Rosa de Copán and Gracias, cattle plains in Choluteca and Olancho (Juticalpa) and vulnerable Caribbean ports at Trujillo and Fort San Fernando de Omoa [@Newson1986; @Vinals2020Outstanding].

Further south, Nicaragua and Costa Rica displayed two sharply contrasting late-colonial trajectories inside a single ecclesiastical and administrative corridor. In Pacific Nicaragua, recovery from sixteenth-century depopulation was anchored by the rival urban axis of administrative León (21,4k in 1820, third-largest city in the entire isthmus) and mercantile Granada (14,2k), flanked by densely populated indigenous and *mestizo* towns across the volcanic plain—Managua (10,4k), Masaya (9,85k), Rivas (8,2k), Chinandega (6,45k) and upland Matagalpa (5,6k) [@Newson1987; @Newson2021Supervivencia]. In Costa Rica, by contrast, the seventeenth-century colonial presence remained tiny, isolated in the eastern Central Valley around Cartago (9,8k by 1820) and coastal Esparza, with enslaved and free Afro-descended workers forming a visible minority on Matina's cacao estates and in Cartago's artisan quarters [@Leon2003Cata]. Only after 1750 did rapid agrarian expansion across the western Central Valley trigger Costa Rica's sustained demographic takeoff: provincial totals more than doubled from 24.536 in 1778 to roughly 60k by 1821 as tobacco-monopoly and smallholder settlements at San José (growing from 2.330 in 1751 to 12,4k in 1820), Heredia (8,4k) and Alajuela (5,4k) eclipsed old colonial Cartago [@PerezBrignoli2010; @HallPerezBrignoli2003].

## Caribbean Enclaves and the Trans-Isthmian Corridor of Panamá

Along the Caribbean margin, colonial demography followed Atlantic geopolitical rivalries rather than Spanish *intendencia* lines. On the Mosquitia Coast, our archival reconstruction places the unreduced indigenous and Zambo-Miskitu population at roughly 42k in 1750, 46k in 1790 and 52k by 1821, clustered along coastal lagoons and river mouths at Sandy Bay (1.820 in 1787), Bluefields (1.850 in 1815), Cabo Gracias a Dios (1.580 in 1787), Pearl Lagoon (1.080), Bilwi (880) and Great Corn Island (680) [@Newson1986; @Newson1987; @Clavel2026King]. Following the 1786 Anglo-Spanish Convention, Britain formally evacuated roughly 2.200 settlers and enslaved workers from the Black River (Palacios) shore settlement in Honduras, transferring most of them directly to British Honduras and boosting Belize's labour force overnight [@SIBBelize2024; @Wainwright2020Colonial].

In British Honduras itself, colonial settlement remained minuscule in headcount yet disproportionate in strategic and ecological impact. Archival muster rolls register 2.656 residents in Belize Town in 1790, 3.824 across the entire Belize settlement in the official 1816 colonial census (over three-quarters enslaved Africans and free people of colour engaged in mahogany cutting and coastal provisioning) and 4.163 in Belize Town by 1820, accompanied by secondary logging and frontier posts at Corozal (920), Orange Walk (840), St. George's Caye (340–480) and the newly founded Garifuna coastal settlement of Stann Creek or Dangriga (480 in 1805, rising to 860 by 1820) [@SIBBelize2024; @Wainwright2020Colonial]. Recurrent late-eighteenth-century droughts documented in colonial Belize from 1771 onward repeatedly disrupted logwood and mahogany river-rafting seasons, forcing reliance on maritime grain imports from Jamaica and North America [@Gali2026Historical].

Across the southern isthmus, the 1778 Panamanian censuses in Table \ref{tab:hgis-subadmin} capture a colony in transition from silver entrepôt to agrarian-pastoral province. Enumerated settled population across the four governorships totalled 59.044 in 1778: 35.955 in the Gobernación de Panamá (including the fertile plains of Natá and Los Santos), 20.061 in Veraguas (including Alanje and Chiriquí), barely 1.762 in malaria-stricken Portobelo after the demise of the galleon fairs, and 1.266 in settled Darién (excluding autonomous Guna and Emberá communities, which lift the full archival benchmark to 68k in 1778 and 92k by 1821) [@JaenSuarez1978]. Provisioning towns in the Pacific savannas—Los Santos (5,6k in 1820), Penonomé, Villa de los Santos, David, Natá and Santiago de Veraguas—supplied rice, beef and maize to Panamá City (9,6k in 1820), demonstrating how indigenous and Afro-Panamanian agro-pastoral adaptations sustained the isthmus long after the silver fleets sailed elsewhere [@JaenSuarez1978; @Aram2021Rice].

## Colonial Urban Hierarchy and Rank-Size Scaling

Across all 190 catalogued settlements active between 1574 and 1820, colonial Central America developed a sharply articulated, primate-led urban network. Figure \ref{fig:guatemala-hierarchy} plots the twelve largest recorded towns alongside the log-log rank-size distribution across all 190 settlements, where the fitted power law over the top 95 urban ranks yields a steep colonial Zipf exponent of $\alpha = 0,90$ ($R^2 = 0,88$, evaluated on the 1774 cross-section).

```{r fig-hierarchy, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/captaincy_general_guatemala_urban_hierarchy.png",
  "Twelve largest catalogued colonial towns (Panel A) and settlement rank-size distribution across 190 Central American, Chiapan and Panamanian settlements showing a steep colonial urban fit ($\\alpha = 0,90$, $R^2 = 0,88$, Panel B), 1524 to 1821.",
  "fig:guatemala-hierarchy"
)
```

Table \ref{tab:top-cities} lists the top 20 colonial settlements from the chapter summary register. Even accounting for the traumatic relocation from Antigua Guatemala (37,5k in 1768) to Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción (31,5k in 1820), the Guatemalan capital exercised unmistakable metropolitan primacy over the Audiencia, standing nearly half again as large as second-ranked León (21,4k) and roughly twice the size of San Salvador (16,5k) and Granada (14,2k) [@Lutz1994; @Juarros1808; @Wortman1982].

```{r tab-top-cities, results='asis'}
top_list <- summary_data$settlement_stats$top_settlements
top_rows <- lapply(seq_along(top_list), function(idx) {
  e <- top_list[[idx]]
  data.frame(
    Rank = as.character(idx),
    Name = clean_label(e$name),
    Country = as.character(e$country),
    Coords = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(round(as.numeric(e$lat), 2L), 2L), ", ", viscount_fmt_number(round(as.numeric(e$lon), 2L), 2L)),
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_number(as.integer(e$peak_pop), 0L),
    PeakYear = as.character(as.integer(e$peak_year)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, top_rows)
rownames(df_top) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Top 20 catalogued colonial settlements across the Captaincy General of Guatemala, Chiapas and Panama ranked by peak recorded population, 1524 to 1821.",
  c("Rank", "Settlement", "Modern Territory", "Lat, Lon", "Peak Pop.", "Peak Year"),
  list(label = "tab:top-cities", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 22L)
)
```

Beneath the four regional capitals stood an evenly graded middle tier of market, highland-tribute and mining towns between 8k and 13,5k inhabitants: Quetzaltenango (13,2k), Cobán (12,4k), fast-rising San José (12,4k), Chamula (11,7k), Santa Ana (10,8k), Managua (10,4k), Masaya (9,85k), Cartago (9,8k), Panamá (9,6k), Totonicapán (9,4k), Comayagua (8,9k), San Miguel (8,9k), Tegucigalpa (8,65k), Heredia (8,4k) and Rivas (8,2k). Combining the top 190 catalogued urban centres at their late-colonial peaks accounts for roughly a fifth to a quarter of the isthmus's total population—confirming that colonial Central America remained an overwhelmingly agrarian and village-based society in which administrative towns functioned primarily as tribute depots, diocesan seats and export-collection hubs rather than industrial centres [@Wortman1982; @HallPerezBrignoli2003].

# Limitations

Five structural constraints qualify demographic reconstructions for colonial Central America between 1524 and 1821.

First, contact-era (1524) baselines carry wide uncertainty bounds ($\pm 25\%$ to $\pm 35\%$). Because Spanish conquerors arrived in Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua after Old World epidemics had already swept ahead of Hernán Cortés's Mexican campaigns, no direct pre-epidemic count exists; early figures must be inferred backward from *tributario* rolls of the 1540s–1550s using household multipliers (typically 3,5 to 4,5 persons per tributary) and archaeological settlement densities [@Lovell1992; @Newson1986; @Newson1987; @Medenou2025Mundo].

Second, late-colonial Bourbon censuses systematically under-enumerated two mobile populations: indigenous villagers who fled *pueblos de indios* into remote mountain ravines (*cimarronaje* or highland flight) to evade head tribute, and *ladino* or *casta* squatters inhabiting dispersed *valles* and cattle *haciendas* outside formal parish oversight [@Osegueda2024Migrar; @HallPerezBrignoli2003]. Archbishop Cortés y Larraz explicitly complained in 1770 that hundreds of rural families across Guatemala and San Salvador lived outside regular sacramental registration—a structural informality in household formation and parish coverage that left enduring statistical legacies across Central America [@Contributors2014Pathways; @Contributors2010Contraceptive].

Third, archival visibility skews heavily toward jurisdictions with surviving Bourbon parish *informes* in the Historical GIS of the Indies. In our 190-settlement gazetteer, Chiapas (95 entries) and Panamá (43 entries) contribute 72,6% of all catalogued sites because village-level 1774 and 1778 rolls survive intact down to small *haciendas* of fewer than 50 persons, whereas Guatemala (11), Nicaragua (13), Honduras (10), El Salvador (7), Costa Rica (6) and Belize (5) are documented primarily at the level of major *cabeceras* and provincial capitals. That sampling difference explains why regional population totals rely on provincial census aggregates rather than raw town summation.

Fourth, as demonstrated in Table \ref{tab:subregion-benchmarks}, global raster-kriging surfaces exhibit spatial spillover across narrow cordilleran borders, inflating 1820 estimates for thinly inhabited Caribbean lowlands (British Honduras and Mosquitia) while depressing compact highland-volcanic cores (San Salvador and Guatemala). Future high-resolution terrain-weighted kriging incorporating elevation and rainfall barriers will sharpen sub-regional raster concordance without altering the overall 1,25M–1,42M isthmian envelope.

Fifth, non-Spanish populations in unreduced Atlantic territories—autonomous Guna and Emberá groups in Darién, interior Sumu and Pech bands in Taguzgalpa and Tologalpa, and transient enslaved or Garifuna maritime communities along the Gulf of Honduras—escaped regular decennial registration, leaving their colonial totals bounded by missionary reports, British colonial correspondence and ethnohistorical carrying-capacity estimates [@Newson1986; @Wainwright2020Colonial; @Clavel2026King].

# Conclusion

Between 1524 and 1821, the Captaincy General of Guatemala, British Honduras and the Audiencia of Panamá traversed a complete demographic arc from catastrophic conquest depopulation to sustained late-colonial recovery. From an estimated 4,13M inhabitants at Spanish contact, epidemic mortality, forced labour and slave trafficking drove the isthmus down by roughly 82% to a colonial nadir near 742k around 1650 [@MacLeod1973; @Lovell1992; @Newson1986; @Newson1987]. Over the ensuing 170 years, natural increase, highland indigenous resilience and accelerating ethnic admixture lifted aggregate numbers back to 1,42M on archival provincial benchmarks in 1821 (and 1,25M–1,34M on raster-kriged surfaces between 1800 and 1820), still barely a third of pre-conquest levels yet firmly launched onto an upward nineteenth-century growth curve [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Wortman1982].

Equally enduring was the geographic and social restructuring forged during those three centuries. Spanish colonial rule concentrated population along the Pacific volcanic chain and cool Mesoamerican highlands—from Chiapas and Guatemala through indigo-rich San Salvador to León, Granada and the expanding Central Valley of Costa Rica—while leaving the Caribbean coast fractured between the autonomous Mosquito Kingdom, the British timber enclave of Belize, newly arrived Garifuna coastal towns and the quiet maritime corridor of Portobelo and Darién [@Juarros1808; @JaenSuarez1978; @SIBBelize2024; @PerezBrignoli2010]. When Central America declared independence in 1821, it inherited not a unified demographic plain, but a sharply polarised archipelago of highland indigenous *pueblos*, mixed-race Pacific export basins and Atlantic frontier enclaves whose regional contrasts continue to shape isthmian demography two centuries later.

# Appendix

## Decadal Raster-Integrated Population Evolution (1600 to 1820)

Table \ref{tab:raster-evolution} reports the decadal raster-kriged population trajectories across all eight jurisdictions and the isthmian domain total at six benchmark dates between 1600 and 1820, together with final 1820 raster densities in inhabitants per km².

```{r tab-raster-evolution, results='asis'}
ev_rows <- lapply(subregions, function(r) {
  tr <- r$trajectory
  data.frame(
    Subregion = clean_label(r$name),
    Y1600 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1600"]])),
    Y1700 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1700"]])),
    Y1750 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1750"]])),
    Y1780 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1780"]])),
    Y1800 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1800"]])),
    Y1820 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1820"]])),
    Dens = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(r$end_density_km2), 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_ev <- do.call(rbind, ev_rows)
dt <- summary_data$domain_trajectory
df_ev_tot <- data.frame(
  Subregion = "Domain Total (682.861 km²)",
  Y1600 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dt[["1600"]])),
  Y1700 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dt[["1700"]])),
  Y1750 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dt[["1750"]])),
  Y1780 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dt[["1780"]])),
  Y1800 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dt[["1800"]])),
  Y1820 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dt[["1820"]])),
  Dens = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(dt[["1820"]]) / tot_area, 2L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_ev <- rbind(df_ev, df_ev_tot)
rownames(df_ev) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_ev,
  "Raster-integrated population trajectories (1600 to 1820) and 1820 raster density (inhabitants per km²) across eight colonial isthmian jurisdictions.",
  c("Colonial Jurisdiction", "1600", "1700", "1750", "1780", "1800", "1820", "1820 Dens."),
  list(label = "tab:raster-evolution", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Territorial Distribution of the 190 Catalogued Colonial Settlements

Table \ref{tab:country-breakdown} summarises the distribution of the 190 catalogued colonial settlements across modern national territories, reflecting the dense village-level preservation of 1774–1796 Chiapan and 1778 Panamanian parish rolls alongside major colonial *cabeceras* across Central America and Belize.

```{r tab-country-breakdown, results='asis'}
cc <- unlist(summary_data$settlement_stats$country_counts)
cc_ord <- sort(cc, decreasing = TRUE)
df_cc <- data.frame(
  Territory = names(cc_ord),
  Sites = vapply(as.integer(cc_ord), function(v) viscount_fmt_number(v, 0L), character(1)),
  Share = vapply(100 * as.integer(cc_ord) / n_sites, function(v) paste0(viscount_fmt_number(v, 1L), "%"), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_cc <- rbind(df_cc, data.frame(
  Territory = "Total Catalogued Settlements",
  Sites = viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L),
  Share = "100%",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
))
rownames(df_cc) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_cc,
  "Distribution of 190 catalogued colonial settlements across eight modern national territories, 1524 to 1821.",
  c("Modern Territory", "Catalogued Settlements", "Share of Gazetteer"),
  list(label = "tab:country-breakdown", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Footnotes

**Note 1 (Jurisdictional Inclusion of Chiapas and Panamá).** Throughout the colonial period (1549 to 1821), the Alcaldía Mayor and later Intendencia of Ciudad Real de Chiapas formed an integral province of the Captaincy General of Guatemala; its formal transfer to Mexico occurred only after the 1824 plebiscite following the collapse of the First Mexican Empire. Conversely, the Audiencia of Panamá (Panamá, Veraguas and Darién) answered judicially to Peru and after 1739 to the Viceroyalty of New Granada, yet is analysed here alongside Guatemala to preserve unbroken geographical coverage of the Central American isthmus.

**Note 2 (Dual-Series Reconciliation).** Archival provincial totals in Table \ref{tab:subregion-benchmarks} (summing to 4,13M in 1524, 742k in 1650 and 1,42M in 1821) represent historical-demographic benchmarks calibrated to Bourbon censuses and regional monographs, whereas raster-integrated decadal values in Figure \ref{fig:guatemala-trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:raster-evolution} (519k in 1600 to 1,25M in 1820) represent equal-area integrations of the continuous gridded substratum across the 682.861 km² jurisdictional mask.

**Note 3 (Antigua Guatemala and Nueva Guatemala Continuity).** Following the Santa Marta earthquake of 29 July 1773, the royal capital relocated roughly 25 km northeast from Santiago de Guatemala (Antigua) to Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción (Ciudad de Guatemala) in 1776. Both cities are retained as distinct geocoded entities in the settlement register so that Antigua's post-earthquake contraction (37,5k in 1768 to 11,2k in 1808) and the new capital's rapid growth (23.434 in 1778 to 31,5k in 1820) remain transparently tracked without double-counting urban residents.
